summary: myidsan gains FIDO2/WebAuthn security keys as a second factor alongside TOTP: a user may hold either or both, and the login gate accepts whichever is presented. New infra/webauthn wraps github.com/go-webauthn/webauthn (new dependency) to resolve the Relying Party ID and allowed origin from the incoming request when unconfigured (host with port stripped, scheme from r.TLS, never from the client's Origin header), requests 'none' attestation, and does not require a resident/discoverable credential so older hardware keys with limited slots still work. Self-service enrol/list/rename/delete lives on the Profile page's new 'Security keys' card (GET/POST/PUT/DELETE /api/mfa/webauthn); a superadmin can clear another account's keys entirely at DELETE /api/mfa-admin/{id}/webauthn, gated by the same step-up re-authentication as a TOTP admin-reset. On the sign-in side, the pre-session MFA challenge now ORs both factor kinds and reports which ones a specific account holds via a new mfaMethods field, so the login screen prompts for a code, a key, or a choice rather than assuming TOTP; two new PUBLIC legs (POST /api/login/mfa/webauthn/begin and /finish) run the two-round-trip assertion ceremony while preserving the existing invariant that no session cookie is issued until the second factor is proven. The identical challenge now also renders on the server-rendered /api/auth/login page (a 'Use a security key' button driven by inline vanilla JS calling the same two endpoints), which is where every relying app's SSO hop lands, myseliasan included. Building that page's support caught and fixed a real bypass introduced by shipping WebAuthn: that handler's MFA challenger had been wired with the TOTP service only, so an account whose ONLY enrolled factor was a security key would have cleared that page's gate with no second factor checked at all, on every relying app in the suite. Account deletion now also removes an account's TOTP factor and every enrolled security key (previously TOTP rows were harmlessly orphaned, but a WebAuthn credential id is unique across the whole table, so an orphaned row would have silently refused to let that same physical key be re-enrolled to a recreated account later). A signature counter that fails to advance is the spec's documented clone signal, but most platform authenticators and every synced passkey legitimately report 0 forever, so that ambiguous case is accepted rather than refused, flagged on the credential row, and written to the audit trail (webauthn.clone_warning) instead of locking out working hardware. Backup & restore now carries enrolled security keys inside the existing 'mfa' section; the first draft of that leg held the raw entity and silently dropped the public key on marshal (PublicKey is json:"-"), which would have restored cleanly and then failed every assertion — fixed with a backupWebauthnCredential wrapper, covered by a regression test. Verified end-to-end using Chrome's CDP virtual authenticator (real key-pair, real attestation/assertion signatures checked server-side): enrol from Profile, sign out, password sign-in, challenge advertises mfaMethods, complete with the key, session issued; and separately on the server-rendered login page, confirming the key button appears with no code field for a key-only account. The sign-counter/clone-warning branch (unreachable without real hardware) and Active Directory/Samba AD account interplay specifically are not yet exercised.
compatibility: Adds one new table (user_webauthn_credential), one new config block (webauthn — Enabled is a pointer that defaults ON, safe because enrolment is strictly per-user opt-in and an account with no key behaves exactly as before), and a new go-webauthn/webauthn v0.17.4 dependency. No existing account, session, or config is affected until a user chooses to enrol a key. WebAuthn requires a secure context (HTTPS, or localhost), so the feature is simply unavailable over plain HTTP on any other host; nothing else in the login flow changes for accounts with no key enrolled. A restore of an .idbackup archive onto a host that will not share the original hostname must set webauthn.relyingPartyId explicitly in config.json first, or every restored security key will be refused by the browser (the credential is bound to the Relying Party ID it was created under; this is not editable from the Settings page, which does not yet cover the webauthn block).
